title: Uppalavanna
hookLine: foremost in psychic power among the nuns, and a survivor of terrible harm, told with care

lines: HER LIFE IS NOT THE HARM.
cards: Two names. In a short passage of the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha names two nuns as the measure for his nuns: a nun of faith may hope to become like Khema and like Uppalavanna. Khema came yesterday.
Today is the other. Her name, tradition says, comes from the blue lotus, the color of her skin. The texts remember her for power.
The commentaries also remember a harm done to her that no one should ever suffer. Today touches it once, gently, and spends longer on who she was before it and after it. Her life is not the harm.

teach.b: First, who she is. In the list of foremost disciples, Uppalavanna is named first among the nuns for psychic power, what the texts call iddhi. That title comes from the Buddha.

teach.h: A HARM, AND IT WAS HIS.
teach.b: Second, the harm, told the way the Dhammapada commentary tells it, and no further. She was living alone in a forest hut. A man who had long wanted her hid there and forced himself on her.
She was already awakened, the story says. The deed was his, and the story treats it as his alone. Tradition says the earth opened and took him.
Third, what came after. Some monks wondered aloud whether an awakened person might still take pleasure in such things.
The Buddha answered that the awakened cling to sense pleasures no more than water clings to a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed to the point of a needle. She was not stained.
And something practical changed: tradition says the Buddha asked that nuns no longer live alone in the forest, and King Pasenadi had a dwelling built for them inside the town. Fourth, her own voice.
In the Connected Discourses, Mara, the tempter, finds her standing alone under a sal tree in full flower, and asks if she isn't afraid of rogues. She is not, she answers.
She has mastered her mind, and he can't frighten her. That's the Uppalavanna the texts keep: not only what was done to her, but who she was, before and after.

how: In the Theravada tradition, Khema and Uppalavanna are remembered together as the Buddha's chief women disciples, and the story of Uppalavanna's forest hut is told as the reason nuns were given a dwelling in town.

o: a nun foremost in psychic power
the Buddha's foster mother, the first nun

games.q: you're Uppalavanna, standing alone under a flowering sal tree. Mara appears and asks if you aren't afraid of rogues. what do you say?
o: admit you're afraid and hurry back to town.
say no: you've mastered your mind, and he can't frighten you.
say nothing and wait for him to go.
games.why: she tells Mara she is not afraid: her mind is mastered, and he can't frighten her. Mara is the one who leaves.

practice: Hold in mind someone who came through something hard that was not their fault; you don't need the details, those are theirs.

Picture the whole person, their laugh, their skill, the way they are now, and if wishing them well comes easily, let it come. If this brushes against something of your own, it's enough to keep breathing, slowly and steadily.

wordCard.voice: Uppalavanna. The nun named foremost in psychic power, who survived harm that was never hers, and met Mara unafraid. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Uppalavanna: tradition links the name to the blue lotus, uppala, the color of her skin.

carryVoice: Your line: she survived. A life is always more than its wound. See you tomorrow.
